questions: What is an IBM MQ queue manager?
The server component that owns queues and other MQ objects, provides messaging services to applications, and manages logs and recovery
Queue managers host queues, channels, listeners and other objects. They manage persistence through logs and queue files and provide transactional messaging.
Correct: the queue manager is MQ's core server.
QM1 hosts ORDERS.IN and PAYMENTS.OUT queues for the retail applications.
Everything in MQ lives in a queue manager.
What is a local queue in IBM MQ?
A queue owned by the queue manager the application is connected to, which physically holds messages
A pointer to a queue on another queue manager
Local queues store messages on the owning queue manager. Remote queue definitions, alias queues and model queues are other types.
Correct: a local queue holds messages.
Wrong: that is a remote queue definition.
Local holds messages; remote definitions point elsewhere.
What does a remote queue definition (QREMOTE) do?
It is a local definition that directs messages to a queue on another queue manager through a transmission queue and channel
QREMOTE names the remote queue and queue manager. Messages put to it go to the transmission queue and are moved by a sender channel.
Correct: it routes to a remote queue.
Wrong: it holds no messages itself.
Application puts to PAY.TO.HUB (QREMOTE) -> XMITQ HUB -> channel -> HUB.PAY.IN on QMHUB.
QREMOTE + XMITQ + SDR/RCVR channels = point-to-point distributed queuing.
Which channel type do client applications use to connect to a queue manager over the network?
Client applications connect through SVRCONN channels (the client side uses CLNTCONN definitions or connection parameters). Sender and receiver channels connect queue managers to each other.
Wrong: queue manager to queue manager.
Wrong: queue manager to queue manager.
APP.SVRCONN with TLS and CHLAUTH rules accepts connections from payment microservices.
Client channels: SVRCONN/CLNTCONN. Queue manager channels: SDR/RCVR and CLUSSDR/CLUSRCVR.
What happens to a persistent message when the queue manager restarts unexpectedly?
It survives the restart because it is logged and recovered by the queue manager
Persistent messages are written to the recovery log and restored after a restart or failure (assuming storage integrity). Non-persistent messages are typically lost on restart.
Wrong: that is the non-persistent case.
Payment instructions are sent as persistent so they survive a pod restart.
What is the dead-letter queue (DLQ) used for in IBM MQ?
Holding messages that cannot be delivered to their destination (for example the target queue is full or does not exist), with a dead-letter header describing the reason

When a queue manager (often a receiving channel) cannot deliver a message, it puts it on the DLQ with an MQDLH header containing the reason code. A dead-letter handler (runmqdlq) can retry or route these messages.
Correct: the DLQ holds undeliverable messages.
Messages for a full queue on the receiving queue manager land on its DLQ with reason MQRC_Q_FULL.
DLQ = undeliverable. Backout queue = repeatedly failing processing.
A receiver channel stops with an error because a target queue is full, blocking all traffic on that channel. What prevents this?
Defining a dead-letter queue on the receiving queue manager so undeliverable messages are moved aside and the channel keeps running
Without a DLQ, a receiving channel that cannot deliver a message cannot continue. With a DLQ, the problem message is set aside and other messages keep flowing.
Correct: a DLQ keeps channels flowing.
Wrong: risks data loss and does not address the issue.
ALTER QMGR DEADQ(SYSTEM.DEAD.LETTER.QUEUE) on every queue manager is a standard rule.
Always define a DLQ on queue managers that receive messages from channels.
Which statement about message ordering in IBM MQ is MOST accurate?

Messages put by a single application in the same unit-of-work context to a single queue are retrieved in order (FIFO by priority) when there is a single consumer; multiple consumers or different paths can break overall ordering
MQ guarantees global ordering across all queue managers and consumers
Order is guaranteed only for non-persistent messages

MQ preserves order for one producer to one queue to one consumer (within priority). Concurrent consumers, priorities, rollbacks or multiple routes can change the effective order. Message groups support ordered sets.
Correct: order depends on single producer and consumer paths.
Wrong: no global ordering across consumers.
Wrong: order is preserved in simple cases.
Wrong: persistence does not determine order.
To keep order per account, the design routes each account to one queue consumed by a single instance.
Ordering breaks with parallel consumers. Design for it explicitly.
What is the main purpose of an MQ cluster (not to be confused with HA clustering)?
Simplified administration of interconnected queue managers and workload balancing of messages across multiple instances of a clustered queue
Replicating messages so they survive a queue manager failure

MQ clusters reduce channel and definition administration and can distribute messages across several queue managers hosting the same queue. They do NOT replicate messages; HA needs Native HA, multi-instance or a similar mechanism.
Wrong: MQ clusters do not replicate messages.
Three queue managers host ORDERS.IN in cluster RETAIL; senders' messages are balanced across them.
MQ cluster is not HA. Messages on a failed queue manager wait until it recovers.
How many full repository queue managers are recommended in an MQ cluster?
Two, for availability of cluster information
Every queue manager should be a full repository
Two full repositories provide redundancy for cluster topology information. More can add administrative complexity, and one is a single point of failure for changes.
Wrong: a single point of failure.
QMFR1 and QMFR2 are full repositories; application queue managers are partial repositories.
Two full repositories, defined with manual CLUSSDR channels to each other.
What is an MQ 'uniform cluster' designed for?
A set of near-identical queue managers where MQ automatically rebalances connected client applications across members for scale and availability
A single queue manager with three replicas
In uniform clusters, applications connect with the same CCDT, and MQ rebalances application instances across the queue managers to keep load even, including after a member restarts.
Correct: automatic application rebalancing across identical queue managers.
Wrong: uniform clusters use cluster channels.
Twelve instances of an app spread automatically across four uniform cluster queue managers, 3 per member.
Native HA = availability of one queue manager. Uniform cluster = horizontal scale across queue managers.
Which MQ availability option in CP4I runs three replicas of a queue manager, each with its own storage, and replicates log data between them?
Native HA uses three pods, each with its own RWO volume. One is active and two are replicas that receive log data; if the active fails, a replica takes over.
Wrong: multi-instance uses shared file storage (RWX) and two pods.
availability.type: NativeHA in the QueueManager CR deploys qm-ibm-mq-0/1/2.
Native HA = RWO block per replica. Multi-instance = shared RWX file system.
Which TWO statements about multi-instance queue managers in CP4I are correct? (Select TWO.)
They use two pods (active and standby) sharing the queue manager data on a shared file system (RWX)
The shared file system must support correct file locking (for example NFSv4 with lease-based locking)
They require three replicas with RWO volumes
They do not require persistent storage
Multi-instance relies on shared storage and file locks. If locking is unreliable, both instances could believe they are active, risking data corruption.
Correct: active/standby with shared RWX storage.
Wrong: persistent shared storage is required.
A multi-instance queue manager uses an NFSv4 storage class certified for MQ's locking requirements.
Multi-instance = shared file system plus locking integrity.
An application gets MQRC 2035 (MQRC_NOT_AUTHORIZED) when connecting to a queue manager in CP4I. Which areas should be checked?
CHLAUTH rules on the channel, connection authentication (CONNAUTH, user ID and password or certificate mapping), and object authority records (AUTHREC) for the asserted user

2035 means the connection or operation was not authorized. Common causes are a CHLAUTH block (for example the default rule blocking privileged users), failed connection authentication, or missing authority for the mapped user on the queue manager or queue.
Correct: CHLAUTH, CONNAUTH and OAM authorities.
The queue manager error log shows AMQ9777E: channel was blocked by CHLAUTH rule; adding a USERMAP rule fixed it.
2035 -> read the queue manager error log; it names the exact security check that failed.
An application receives MQRC 2053 (MQRC_Q_FULL) when putting messages. What is the cause and the right fix?
The queue reached MAXDEPTH, usually because consumers are slow or stopped; fix the consumer backlog first, then adjust MAXDEPTH and alerting if justified
The queue manager is in Native HA
Q_FULL means the queue has reached its maximum depth. The root cause is usually consumption: a consumer that is down, slow or blocked. Increasing MAXDEPTH alone can hide the problem.
Correct: address consumption, then capacity and monitoring.
The consumer pod was crash-looping; once fixed, the 50,000-message backlog drained in minutes.
Queue depth alerts should fire well before MAXDEPTH.
Which combination provides 'once and once only' assured delivery semantics in IBM MQ?
Persistent messages put and got within units of work (syncpoint), with transactional handling by the application

MQ's assured delivery comes from persistent messages plus transactional put and get. If the consumer fails before committing, the message is rolled back and redelivered; it is not lost or duplicated by MQ.
Wrong: Kafka setting with no guarantees.
A payments consumer gets under syncpoint, writes to the ledger (XA), then commits.
Assured delivery = persistent + syncpoint (+ XA with resources).
What is Advanced Message Security (AMS) in IBM MQ used for?
End-to-end protection of message payloads (signing and/or encryption) from the putting application to the getting application, including while at rest on queues

AMS protects message content end to end with policies (integrity, privacy, confidentiality). This protects data at rest on queues and as it passes through intermediate queue managers, not just on the wire.
Card data on PAY.CARD.IN is encrypted by AMS so even MQ administrators cannot read the payload.
TLS protects channels in transit; AMS protects messages end to end.
An application receives MQRC 2009 (MQRC_CONNECTION_BROKEN) intermittently when connecting to a Native HA queue manager in OpenShift during failovers. What should be implemented?
Automatic client reconnection (for example MQCNO_RECONNECT or a reconnect option in the client configuration) with a CCDT or connection list, plus application retry logic

During failover the active instance changes, and connections to the failed instance break. Client auto-reconnect, which works through the Service or route pointing at the active instance, and proper retry handling make failovers transparent or brief.
JMS clients set the reconnect option and reconnect timeout so failovers cause only a pause of a few seconds.
HA on the server needs reconnect logic on the client.
A bank needs MQ high availability within a region (zone failure) AND disaster recovery to a second region with minimal data loss. Which design is MOST appropriate in CP4I?

Native HA queue managers spread across three zones for in-region HA, plus a DR mechanism to the second region such as Native HA cross-region replication (available in recent MQ 9.4 releases, so verify version support) or storage/backup-based replication, with documented RPO/RTO and client reconnection to the DR endpoint
Use an MQ cluster across regions as the DR mechanism
Use a multi-instance queue manager stretched across regions on one NFS share
Rely on Kubernetes to recreate the queue manager in the other region with empty storage

HA and DR are separate layers. Native HA covers zone failure. A cross-region mechanism is needed for regional failure, either the asynchronous Native HA replication between Native HA groups in recent MQ versions, or storage or backup replication. Each has its own RPO.
Correct: layered HA plus DR, with version awareness.
Wrong: MQ clusters do not replicate messages.
Wrong: latency and shared storage across regions are unsuitable.
The Frankfurt Native HA group replicates asynchronously to the recovery group in Amsterdam, and the runbook promotes the recovery group during a regional outage.
Always identify the HA scope (zone versus region) and the replication mode (sync versus async).
How can MQ objects (queues, channels, authority records) be defined declaratively for a queue manager in CP4I?
Provide MQSC (and INI) in ConfigMaps or Secrets referenced by the QueueManager CR, so they are applied when the queue manager starts
Only by running commands manually in each pod
The QueueManager CR can reference MQSC and INI from ConfigMaps or Secrets. This makes the configuration reproducible and version-controlled.
Correct: declarative MQSC through CR references.
Wrong: manual changes are not reproducible.
Git holds qm1-mqsc ConfigMap content; Argo CD applies it with the QueueManager CR.
GitOps for MQ = CR + MQSC ConfigMaps.
A message must be delivered to many subscribers interested in a topic, and new subscribers do not need past messages. Which MQ capability is appropriate?
MQ publish/subscribe with topics and (durable or non-durable) subscriptions
Point-to-point queues with copies made by the producer
MQ supports publish/subscribe: publishers put to a topic, and the queue manager delivers copies to each subscription. Durable subscriptions keep messages while subscribers are disconnected.
Wrong: the producer would have to know every consumer.
Price updates are published to topic PRICES/EQUITY and delivered to trading desks' durable subscriptions.
MQ pub/sub = fan-out without replay. Kafka = fan-out with replay.
What is a transmission queue (XMITQ) in IBM MQ?
A local queue that temporarily holds messages destined for a remote queue manager until a sender channel transfers them
Messages destined for other queue managers are placed on the transmission queue. The sender channel reads from it and transmits to the receiver.
XMITQ QMHUB depth rises during a network outage and drains when the channel restarts.
After enabling TLS on a SVRCONN channel, clients fail with MQRC 2393 (MQRC_SSL_INITIALIZATION_ERROR) or 2397. Which items should be checked?

The CipherSpec matches on client and channel, the client trusts the queue manager's CA, the client keystore (and certificate, if mutual TLS) is configured correctly, and the queue manager has its certificate label configured
TLS errors in MQ usually come from CipherSpec mismatch, missing trust, a misconfigured keystore, or an incorrect certificate label. The queue manager error log (AMQ9xxx) gives specifics.
Correct: CipherSpec, trust, keystore and labels.
The JMS client lacked the corporate root CA in its truststore; adding it fixed 2397.
MQ TLS errors: AMQ9631 (CipherSpec mismatch), AMQ9633 (bad certificate), and so on.
IBM's enterprise distribution of Apache Kafka, deployed and managed by an operator on OpenShift, with additional tooling (UI, schema registry, geo-replication, security)
Event Streams provides Kafka with enterprise features: operator-based lifecycle, a management UI, security, monitoring, a schema registry, geo-replication and Kafka Connect support.
An EventStreams CR deploys a 3-broker Kafka cluster with an external SCRAM listener and the schema registry.
In Kafka, what is a topic partition?
An ordered, append-only log that forms the unit of parallelism and ordering within a topic
A copy of a queue manager
Topics are split into partitions. Each partition is ordered, and consumers in a group divide partitions among themselves for parallel processing.
Correct: the partition is the unit of order and parallelism.
Topic orders has 12 partitions, so up to 12 consumers in one group can work in parallel.
Ordering is per partition, not per topic.
What is a Kafka consumer group?
A set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic, with each partition assigned to only one consumer in the group
Consumer groups give scalable consumption. Each partition is consumed by exactly one member of the group, and offsets are tracked per group.
Wrong: producers are not grouped this way.
The fraud-scoring and billing groups each read every orders event independently.
Different groups = independent copies. Same group = shared work.
What does the Kafka replication factor of a topic define?
How many copies of each partition are stored on different brokers
With replication factor 3, each partition has a leader and two followers on different brokers. This lets the partition survive broker failures.
Correct: the number of partition replicas.
Wrong: consumers are not limited by RF.
Wrong: retention is a separate setting.
Production topics use RF=3 across three zones.
What does 'retention.ms' configure on a Kafka topic?
How long records are kept before becoming eligible for deletion (for delete cleanup policy), regardless of whether they were consumed
How long a consumer can take to process a message
Kafka retains records based on time or size limits, independent of consumption. This enables replay and multiple consumers.
Audit events keep 30 days of history for replay.
Kafka keeps data after consumption. MQ removes it on get.
A consumer group has 12 consumers but the topic has 6 partitions. What happens?
Only 6 consumers receive partitions; the other 6 stay idle
A partition is assigned to one consumer per group. Consumers beyond the partition count are idle (and act as standby).
Wrong: a partition is not shared within a group.
Wrong: partitions are not created automatically.
Increasing partitions to 12 lets all consumers work, but key-to-partition mapping changes for new records.
Max consumer parallelism per group = number of partitions.
Which producer settings give the strongest durability for important events in Event Streams?
acks=all with idempotence enabled, and a topic with RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=2
acks=all waits until all in-sync replicas acknowledge, and min ISR=2 ensures at least two copies before acknowledgement. Idempotence prevents duplicates on retries.
Payment events use acks=all and enable.idempotence=true; topics enforce min.insync.replicas=2.
Durability trio: acks=all + RF=3 + min ISR=2.
Producers using acks=all receive NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS errors after one of three brokers fails. The topic has RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=3. What is the issue?
min.insync.replicas=3 requires all three replicas, so losing any broker blocks writes; set min.insync.replicas=2 to tolerate one failure
With min ISR equal to RF, any broker loss makes the partition unwritable for acks=all producers. RF=3 with min ISR=2 balances durability and availability.
Correct: min ISR is too strict.
Changing min.insync.replicas to 2 allowed writes to continue during broker maintenance.
min ISR = RF means zero fault tolerance for writes.
Consumer lag on a topic grows steadily during business hours. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
Consumers cannot keep up; add consumers (up to the partition count), increase partitions if needed, or optimize processing
The topic retention is too long
Lag is the gap between the latest offset and the committed offset. Growing lag means consumption throughput is below production throughput.
Wrong: retention does not cause lag.
Wrong: does not cause lag on its own.
Scaling the consumer deployment from 3 to 6 (with 6 partitions) eliminated the lag.
Lag is the key consumer health metric.
How does a Kafka producer ensure that all events for the same customer go to the same partition?
By setting the record key to the customer ID, so the default partitioner hashes the key to a consistent partition
By using a large batch size
The default partitioner maps a key's hash to a partition, so the same key always lands in the same partition (while the partition count is unchanged), which preserves order per key.
All events for customer C123 go to partition 7 and are processed in order.
Changing the partition count remaps keys. Plan partitions up front.
What is the purpose of the schema registry in Event Streams?
Storing and versioning event schemas (for example Avro) so producers and consumers can serialize and validate data compatibly
A schema registry manages schema versions and compatibility rules, which prevents producers from breaking consumers with incompatible changes. Event Streams provides an Apicurio-based registry.
The OrderCreated Avro schema evolves from v1 to v2 with backward-compatible optional fields.
Schemas + compatibility rules = safe event evolution.
Which approach is recommended to move data continuously from IBM MQ queues into Kafka topics?
Kafka Connect with the IBM MQ source connector, deployed through KafkaConnect and KafkaConnector resources
Kafka Connect provides scalable, fault-tolerant connectors. IBM's MQ source and sink connectors bridge MQ and Kafka, with options for exactly-once delivery in supported versions.
Correct: Kafka Connect plus the MQ source connector.
MQ ORDERS.EVENTS messages stream into Kafka topic orders using the MQ source connector.
MQ to Kafka -> MQ source connector. Kafka to MQ -> MQ sink connector.
Which cleanup policy should be used for a topic that holds the latest state per key (for example customer profile updates) indefinitely?
Log compaction keeps at least the latest record for each key, which suits changelog and state topics.
Correct: compaction keeps the latest value per key.
Topic customer-profiles is compacted so a new service can bootstrap the current state of all customers.
State or changelog -> compact. Events or history -> delete with retention.
A consumer application restarts and reprocesses thousands of events it had already processed. What is the MOST likely cause?
Offsets were not committed (or were committed before processing failed, or auto.offset.reset applied to a new group ID), so consumption resumed from an earlier position

Consumers resume from the last committed offset. If commits are infrequent, disabled, or the group ID changed, the consumer reprocesses or starts from the earliest offset according to auto.offset.reset.
A deployment changed group.id from billing to billing-v2, so the new group started from the earliest offset.
Design consumers to be idempotent; at-least-once is the Kafka default.
An architect needs exactly-once processing from an input topic to an output topic in a Kafka Streams/Flink style pipeline. Which approach is correct?

Use Kafka transactions (transactional.id on the producer, read_committed isolation on consumers) so consumed offsets and produced records commit atomically, or a framework with exactly-once guarantees such as Flink checkpoints with transactional sinks
Kafka exactly-once semantics combine idempotent producers with transactions, so output records and consumer offset commits are atomic. Downstream consumers must use read_committed.
Correct: Kafka transactions or EOS frameworks.
Wrong: duplicates and loss are possible.
An Event Processing (Flink) job uses checkpoints with exactly-once delivery to Kafka.
EOS in Kafka = idempotence + transactions + read_committed.
How are Kafka users and their permissions typically managed in Event Streams?
Through KafkaUser custom resources that define authentication (SCRAM-SHA-512 or mutual TLS) and ACL authorization rules, with credentials generated into Secrets
The operator reconciles KafkaUser resources, creating credentials and ACLs for topics, groups and transactional IDs.
KafkaUser billing-app has read on topic orders and on group billing.
Least privilege: one KafkaUser per application, with scoped ACLs.
A client fails with 'TopicAuthorizationException' when producing to topic orders. Authentication succeeds. What is the cause?
The KafkaUser lacks a write (and describe) ACL on topic orders
The topic has too many partitions
The cluster is out of disk

The SASL handshake succeeded, so the credentials are valid (authentication). The broker then checked the user's ACLs and found no permission to write to the topic (authorization). In Event Streams, ACLs are declared on the KafkaUser resource: producers need Write and Describe on the topic, plus idempotent or transactional permissions if those features are used.
Wrong: that would be a different error.
Wrong: not consistent with successful authentication.
Adding operation Write and Describe on topic orders to the KafkaUser fixed the producer.
Authentication versus authorization errors point to different fixes.
Which TWO statements about Event Streams geo-replication / MirrorMaker 2 are correct? (Select TWO.)
Replication between clusters is asynchronous, so some recent events may not be replicated at the moment of failure (RPO greater than 0)
It can replicate topic data and translate consumer group offsets so consumers can resume in the target cluster
It provides synchronous zero-data-loss replication across regions by default
It replaces the need for replication factor within a cluster
MirrorMaker 2 replicates asynchronously and supports offset translation through checkpoints. In-cluster replication (RF) still protects against broker failure.
Correct: asynchronous, so RPO is greater than 0.
Wrong: in-cluster RF is still needed.
After failover, the billing consumer group resumes from translated offsets in the DR cluster with a few seconds of potential duplicates.
Cross-region Kafka DR = asynchronous, so design consumers to handle duplicates and minor loss.
What does the Kafka Bridge (REST producer and consumer) in Event Streams enable?
HTTP clients to produce and consume Kafka records without a native Kafka client
The bridge provides an HTTP interface to Kafka for clients that cannot use native protocols, such as some IoT devices or legacy applications.
A legacy POS system posts JSON sales events through the REST producer API.
No Kafka client available -> HTTP bridge or REST producer.
How many partitions should an architect choose for a new high-throughput topic?

Based on target throughput divided by per-partition throughput (both producer and consumer), the desired consumer parallelism, key distribution and future growth, while avoiding excessive partitions that add broker overhead
The same as the number of brokers, always

Partition count drives parallelism and throughput but has overhead (file handles, leader elections, memory). Size it from measured throughput, consumer parallelism and growth, because increasing it later remaps keys.
Correct: a capacity-based calculation with headroom.
For 60 MB/s with about 5 MB/s per consumer, plus growth, the team chose 24 partitions.
Partitions are cheap to add but disruptive for keyed ordering. Plan ahead.
What problem does Event Endpoint Management (EEM) solve?
It lets organizations describe, socialize and govern access to Kafka topics as self-service event endpoints, with access enforced by an Event Gateway
EEM provides a catalog where topic owners publish event sources. Consumers discover them, subscribe and receive credentials, and the Event Gateway enforces access and controls.
Correct: governed self-service access to events.
Wrong: that is ACE or DataPower.
Fifty internal teams discover available topics in the EEM catalog instead of emailing the Kafka admin team.
EEM = API management ideas applied to Kafka topics.
In EEM, what do consumers use to connect to a subscribed event endpoint?
Credentials issued by EEM on subscription, used with a Kafka client connecting to the Event Gateway
Direct admin credentials to the Kafka brokers
An API Connect client ID only
When a consumer subscribes, EEM generates credentials scoped to that subscription. The consumer's Kafka client connects to the Event Gateway, which proxies to the underlying cluster.
Correct: subscription credentials via the Event Gateway.
A partner app uses SASL credentials from EEM and the gateway bootstrap address shown in the catalog.
Consumers connect to the Event Gateway, not to the brokers.
What does an EEM 'option' (exposure option) on a topic define?
How a topic is exposed to consumers, including controls such as approval requirements, quotas, redaction of fields or schema filtering

Owners can offer several options for the same topic, each with different controls, similar to API plans. For example, an option with a redacted payload for external partners and a full one for internal teams.
Correct: options define how a topic is exposed.
Option 'partner-redacted' removes customer email fields; 'internal-full' requires approval.
EEM options are like plans for events.
A topic contains customer PII, and some subscribers must not see email addresses. How can EEM help?
Apply a redaction control on the exposure option so the Event Gateway removes or masks specified fields for those subscribers
Create a separate Kafka cluster per subscriber
Tell subscribers not to read the field
EEM controls enforced at the Event Gateway can redact sensitive fields per option, so one topic can be shared safely with different audiences.
Marketing receives order events without email or phone fields; fulfilment receives the full events.
Data minimization at the gateway is a core EEM governance feature.
Which TWO benefits does exposing topics through the EEM Event Gateway provide over giving partners direct broker access? (Select TWO.)
The internal Kafka cluster's brokers are not exposed directly; the gateway enforces subscription-based access
Per-subscription controls such as quotas and approval can be enforced and revoked centrally
Partners can create topics on the internal cluster
The gateway gives network and security separation plus central, revocable, per-subscription governance.
Revoking a partner's subscription in EEM immediately blocks its gateway access.
How do developers discover event sources in EEM?
By browsing the EEM catalog, which shows topic descriptions, sample messages and schemas, and exports AsyncAPI documentation
The catalog documents each event endpoint with descriptions, schemas, samples and AsyncAPI, which enables discovery and self-service.
Correct: the EEM catalog provides discovery.
A developer finds 'shipment-status' in the catalog, downloads its AsyncAPI, and generates client code.
AsyncAPI is to events what OpenAPI is to REST APIs.
A subscribed consumer can connect to the Event Gateway but receives authorization errors when consuming. Other subscribers work. What should be checked?

That the consumer uses the credentials for the correct subscription and option, the subscription is approved and active, and the topic name or alias and consumer group settings match what the option allows
Gateway access is scoped by subscription. Wrong credentials, a pending or revoked subscription, or an unexpected topic alias leads to authorization failures for that consumer only.
The consumer was using credentials from an expired subscription; renewing access fixed it.
One consumer failing while others succeed -> look at that subscription.

A company wants to offer the same Kafka events to internal teams with full payloads and to external partners with redacted payloads and rate limits, while keeping partners out of the internal network. Which architecture is MOST appropriate?

One EEM manager with two Event Gateway groups: an internal gateway and an external gateway in a DMZ; topics are exposed with different options (full versus redacted and quota-controlled) mapped to the appropriate gateway groups
Two separate copies of the topic produced by every producer
Direct broker access for internal teams and partners
Export topic data nightly to files

EEM supports multiple gateway groups and options. The network separation (DMZ gateway) and the governance controls (redaction, quotas) together meet both audiences' needs without duplicating producers.
Correct: gateway groups plus differentiated options.
Wrong: duplicates effort and risks inconsistency.
Wrong: no governance, and exposes internal brokers.
The partner gateway runs in the DMZ cluster and enforces 100 messages per second per subscription with PII redaction.
Different audiences -> different options and gateway placements.
How does EEM relate to API Connect in CP4I?

They are complementary: API Connect manages REST/SOAP APIs and the DataPower gateway, while EEM manages Kafka event endpoints and the Event Gateway, so together they give consistent governance across APIs and events
API Connect manages Kafka topics natively without EEM
Both apply product-style management (catalog, subscriptions, controls) to different interface types: APIs and events.
Wrong: EEM is the Kafka endpoint manager.
A partner programme offers both a REST shipment API (API Connect) and a shipment-events stream (EEM).
Synchronous interfaces -> API Connect. Asynchronous Kafka interfaces -> EEM.
A topic owner wants to require approval before any new subscriber can consume a sensitive topic. What should be configured?
An approval control on the topic's exposure option in EEM
Approval controls make new subscriptions wait until the owner approves them, which gives human governance over sensitive data.
New requests for 'payments-events' notify the data owner for approval.
Which statement about the Event Gateway is correct?
It speaks the Kafka protocol, so consumers and producers use standard Kafka clients against it, and it applies EEM policy before proxying to the backing cluster
It stores the topic data permanently
It is only an HTTP proxy

The Event Gateway implements the Kafka wire protocol. Standard Kafka clients connect to it exactly as they would to a broker, using the bootstrap address and credentials issued by EEM. The gateway applies the subscription's controls (quotas, redaction, schema filtering) and then proxies requests to the backing cluster, so applications need no proprietary SDK and the brokers are never exposed directly.
Correct: Kafka protocol proxy with policy enforcement.
Wrong: it handles the Kafka protocol.
An existing Kafka consumer switches to the gateway bootstrap address and EEM credentials with no code changes.
No custom SDK: standard Kafka clients work through the gateway.
What kinds of items are typically stored in the CP4I Automation assets repository?
Reusable integration assets such as API definitions, schemas, message models, flows, mappings and samples

The Automation assets repository (AssetRepository instance) is a design-time catalogue. Teams publish API definitions, schemas, message models, mappings, flows and samples to it, so others can search, preview and reuse them instead of rebuilding. It does not hold runtime data such as logs, Kafka partitions or OS images.
The team publishes OpenAPI documents, DFDL models and canonical JSON schemas for reuse.
How can teams keep the asset repository synchronized with assets maintained in Git?
Configure remote repositories (for example Git) as asset sources so assets are imported and kept up to date in the catalog
The repository can connect to remote Git repositories to import assets, so Git remains the source of truth while the catalog provides discovery.
An assets-catalog Git repository is linked, and new schemas appear in the repository after each merge.
Git = source of truth. Asset repository = discovery layer.
Which TWO governance practices improve the value of a shared asset repository? (Select TWO.)
Consistent metadata (owner, version, domain tags, description) for each asset
Versioning assets and marking deprecated ones clearly
Allowing duplicate assets with no ownership
Removing all descriptions to save space

A shared repository only creates value if people can find assets and trust them. Consistent metadata (owner, domain tags, description, version) makes assets discoverable. Explicit versioning and clear deprecation tell consumers which version is current. Duplicated, ownerless or undocumented assets erode trust and push teams back to building their own.
Correct: metadata aids discovery and ownership.
Correct: versioning and deprecation build trust.
A Customer schema v3 is tagged 'domain:customer', 'owner:crm-team'; v2 is marked deprecated.
Reuse needs trust: ownership + versions + metadata.
Developers report they cannot find an asset that was added to the linked Git repository yesterday. What should be checked FIRST?
Whether the remote repository synchronization succeeded (status, credentials, branch or path configuration) in the asset repository
Assets from remote sources appear after a successful synchronization. Wrong credentials, branch or path configuration block import.
Correct: check the remote sync status and configuration.
The sync was configured for 'main' but the asset was merged to 'develop'.
Missing assets from Git -> check the sync configuration.
Why might an organization prefer the Automation assets repository over a generic file share for integration artefacts?
It provides searchable, typed, versioned integration assets with previews and metadata that integrate with CP4I tooling, which improves discovery and reuse
File shares are not allowed by Kubernetes
It is the only place to store BARs for runtime

A file share stores bytes. The asset repository understands integration asset types: it indexes and previews them, keeps metadata and versions, can synchronize from Git remotes, and integrates with CP4I tooling. That structured discovery is what drives reuse. It does not replace Git as the source of truth, and runtimes can still obtain BAR files from other locations.
Wrong: BARs can be served elsewhere.
Searching 'customer' shows schemas, maps and APIs with previews and owners.
When should an architect choose IBM MQ over Event Streams for a new integration?
When the requirement is assured, transactional, once-only delivery of commands or requests to a specific consumer, often with request/reply and coordination with other transactional resources
When many independent consumers need to replay months of history
When stream processing with windowed aggregations is the core requirement
When analytics teams need a data lake feed
MQ excels at transactional, point-to-point command and request messaging with assured delivery. Kafka excels at high-volume event streams with retention, replay and many consumers.
Wrong: Flink or Event Processing on Kafka.
A 'transfer funds' command goes over MQ; the resulting 'funds transferred' event is published to Kafka.
Native HA queue manager pods show two replicas in 'Replica' state and none active, after a network partition isolated one zone. What is the MOST likely reason?
Only one replica is reachable from a quorum perspective, or the replicas are not synchronized enough to elect a new active; Native HA needs a majority (2 of 3) of connected, in-sync replicas
Native HA always requires 3 active instances
Native HA uses quorum. If the partition leaves fewer than two replicas able to communicate, or the logs are not in sync, no active instance can be elected, which prevents split-brain.
Correct: quorum or synchronization prevents election.
Wrong: only one active instance runs at a time.
Restoring the inter-zone network let the replicas agree and elect an active instance within seconds.
No quorum, no active instance: a safety feature, not a bug.
What is Cruise Control used for in Event Streams?
Rebalancing partitions across brokers (for example after adding brokers or to fix uneven load) using optimization goals, through KafkaRebalance resources
Cruise Control analyses broker load and proposes or executes partition reassignments to balance disk, network and CPU usage.
Wrong: cert-manager or the operator rotates certificates.
After scaling from 3 to 5 brokers, a KafkaRebalance moves partitions onto the new brokers.
Adding brokers does not move existing partitions automatically. Rebalance.
A broker pod's PVC is 95% full, and the broker risks failing. Which actions are appropriate?
Reduce retention (time or size) on large topics, delete unneeded topics, expand the PVC if the storage class supports volume expansion, and add brokers with a rebalance for longer-term capacity
Delete the broker's log directory manually
Disk usage is driven by retention and data volume. Reduce retention, expand volumes (allowVolumeExpansion) and add capacity with rebalancing. Manual deletion corrupts brokers.
Expanding broker PVCs from 500Gi to 1Ti online and cutting debug-topic retention from 30 days to 3 freed capacity.
Kafka disk full is an outage risk, so alert at 70-80%.
What does a model queue enable in IBM MQ?
Dynamic creation of queues (for example temporary reply queues) based on a template
Applications open a model queue to create a dynamic queue, often temporary, for request/reply patterns.
Correct: a template for dynamic queues.
A requester opens SYSTEM.DEFAULT.MODEL.QUEUE to create a temporary reply queue.
Request/reply often uses dynamic reply queues plus correlation IDs.
How do request/reply applications correlate a reply with the original request in IBM MQ?
The requester sets ReplyToQ (and ReplyToQMgr), and the responder copies the request's MsgId (or CorrelId) into the reply's CorrelId, which the requester uses to get the matching reply
Correlation identifiers ensure the requester retrieves the right reply, even when several replies share a queue.
ACE sets the CorrelId from the request MsgId so the API flow gets the right reply within its timeout.
Which Kubernetes custom resource is used in Event Streams to declaratively create a topic?
Topics can be managed declaratively with KafkaTopic resources (partitions, replicas, configuration), which the topic operator reconciles.
GitOps applies KafkaTopic orders with 12 partitions and RF 3.
Topics as code with KafkaTopic CRs.
Which statement about Kafka consumers is correct?
Consumers pull records from brokers and track their position with offsets
Brokers push records to consumers and delete them after delivery
Kafka consumers poll (pull) records and commit offsets. Brokers do not delete records on consumption; retention policies do.
Wrong: Kafka uses a pull model and retention.
Wrong: modern clients do not connect to ZooKeeper.
A consumer polls every 100 ms and commits offsets after successful processing.
Pull plus offsets = consumers control their own pace.
What does the MQ CCDT (Client Channel Definition Table) provide to client applications?
Connection information (channels, hosts, ports, TLS settings) for one or more queue managers, which enables failover and load-balancing lists
A CCDT (binary or JSON) lists client channel definitions. It lets applications connect to alternative queue managers or addresses without code changes.
A JSON CCDT lists qm-a and qm-b, and clients connect to whichever is available.
CCDT externalizes connection details from application code.
An application team wants to produce JSON events but downstream teams want guaranteed structure. What should the architect recommend?
Define a schema (for example Avro or JSON Schema) in the registry with compatibility rules, and use schema-aware serializers so producers cannot publish incompatible data
Schema-enforced serialization with compatibility checks prevents breaking changes and makes structure explicit.
Producers register OrderCreated v1; a v2 that removes a required field is rejected by BACKWARD compatibility.
Contracts for events = schemas + compatibility rules.
